teaser.text: O’Reilly Automotive makes money by buying vehicle parts and supplies, stocking them, and selling them to drivers and repair shops. To understand the business, follow the products, the customers, and the costs that stand between a sale and a profit.

stock.title: O’Reilly stock forecast
stock.meta_description: O’Reilly stock forecast: weighted scenarios, operating drivers, real free cash flow, and what investors pay today.
stock.opening: The weighted price is $87.66 in October 2027 and $101.10 in October 2029. O’Reilly’s forecast hinges on demand, margins and free cash flow.
stock.closing: The full memo also answers how O’Reilly works, who its rivals are, how management allocates capital, and what risks could change the outcome.

blocks.heading: What could O’Reilly’s shares be worth?

paragraphs.text: The weighted price is $87.66 in October 2027, a 2% loss with dividends. It rises to $95.77 in October 2028, a 7% gain. It reaches $101.10 in October 2029, a 13% gain.
The bear case has a 25% weight; the base case has 55%. The bull case carries 20%. The October 2029 range runs from $67.28 in the bear case to $139.28 in the bull case. Today’s price is $89.27.

blocks.heading: What does O’Reilly’s stock forecast depend on?

paragraphs.text: Professional sales grew about 19% from 2023 to 2025, versus about 6% for DIY. Q2 professional comparable sales grew 10%, but DIY transactions fell at a low-single-digit rate while same-item inflation reached 5.5%. Inventory turns also fell from 1.7x to 1.6x. These facts support the base case, but explain the bear and bull separation. The 2024 reserve charge is excluded from the forward run rate.

blocks.heading: How much cash does O’Reilly really make?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash flow records cash produced by the business before capital spending. Free cash flow subtracts spending on stores, distribution, and other capital projects. In 2025, capital spending rose, so less operating cash remained after investment than in the prior year.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for O’Reilly?

paragraphs.text: The price-to-earnings, or P/E, multiple compares the share price with profit per share. Trailing P/E uses the past twelve months; forward P/E uses an estimate of the next twelve. But earnings are an accounting measure, not the same thing as cash available after customers, suppliers, taxes, inventory and new stores have been paid. O’Reilly’s cash-flow yield therefore makes its reinvestment needs central.

blocks.heading: What has O’Reilly guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: The pressure is that price growth is fading. In Q2 2026, same-item inflation contributed 5.5% to average tickets, while DIY transaction counts fell by a low-single-digit percentage. Management expects the inflation benefit to shrink to 1%–2% in the second half of 2026, so O’Reilly will need more visits, parts sold, or professional-shop orders.

blocks.heading: Did O’Reilly keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: The clearest promise is profitable expansion. O’Reilly met its 2025 store-growth target, and its 2026 plan calls for more stores alongside distribution investment. The final test is whether those stores and that network earn returns that justify the cash committed.

blocks.heading: How have O’Reilly’s revenue and profit trended?

paragraphs.text: Revenue, operating income, net income, and diluted earnings per share all rose from the same quarter of 2025. Gross margin held steady. Earnings per share grew faster than net income partly because share repurchases left fewer shares outstanding.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in O’Reilly’s next results?

paragraphs.text: The Q3 2026 results release and conference call should show whether sales hold as the same-item price benefit moderates. They should also show whether DIY transaction counts recover and whether professional-shop demand is strong enough to carry more of the growth.

Cash flow deserves equal attention. O’Reilly must fund stores, distribution capacity, inventory, supplier payments and debt while deciding how much capital to return through buybacks. A strong earnings-per-share result will be less convincing if cash generation falls behind those demands.
